'''Canichana''', or '''Canesi''', is a possible [[language isolate]] of [[Bolivia]] ([[Beni Department|department of Beni]]). In 1991 there were 500 [[Canichana people]], but only 20 spoke the Canichana language; by 2000 the ethnic population was 583, but the language had no mother tongue speakers left. It was spoken on the [[Mamoré River]] and [[Machupo River]].<ref name="Loukotka">{{cite book |last=Loukotka |first=Čestmír |author-link=Čestmír Loukotka |title=Classification of South American Indian languages |url=https://archive.org/details/classificationof0007louk |url-access=registration |publisher=UCLA Latin American Center |year=1968 |location=Los Angeles}}</ref>

== Current situation ==
The Canichana territory is part of the region historically known as [[Mojeños|Moxos]] (or Mojos), which covers approximately 200,000 square kilometers of what is now the department of [[Beni Department|Beni]]. According to data provided in Crevels and Muysken (2009:15), based on the 2001 Census, the Canichana population at that time amounted to 404 members. During the research conducted by Crevels between 1999 and 2001, the author could only find three elders who still remembered some single words and phrases in Kanichana. Regarding the ethnic group, Crevels notes that the Canichanas are mainly engaged in agriculture, with their main agricultural products being cassava, corn, rice, beans and plantains. Part of the harvest is for self-consumption and the other part for local sale. Hunting, fishing and gathering are complementary traditional activities, in addition to the sale of their labor as laborers on the ranches.

== Classification ==
Despite tentative proposals to classify the language, it is generally considered a language isolate or an unclassified language.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Crevels |first=Mily |date=2012 |title=Canichana |url=https://scholar.googleusercontent.com/scholar.bib?q=info:JaviHkrkAZsJ:scholar.google.com/&output=citation&scisdr=ClFwSG4NEKCZ3srkKeM:AFWwaeYAAAAAZmHiMeNqrhZfD9_g2v53NJQP3oA&scisig=AFWwaeYAAAAAZmHiMTHzevX1NGXFzIqt0xRK4eQ&scisf=4&ct=citation&cd=-1&hl=es |journal=Lenguas de Bolivia |volume=2 |pages=415–449}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Markham |first=Clements |date=1910 |title=A List of the Tribes of the Valley of the Amazons, Including Those on the Banks of the Main Stream and of All the Tributaries. |url=https://scholar.googleusercontent.com/scholar.bib?q=info:yuV1HXdT6cMJ:scholar.google.com/&output=citation&scisdr=ClFwSG4NEKCZ3srkv2g:AFWwaeYAAAAAZmHip2h3b_ok29nDHL75TKnpHdE&scisig=AFWwaeYAAAAAZmHip1bLMumH1WyzygzrlN9vnkQ&scisf=4&ct=citation&cd=-1&hl=es |journal=The Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland |volume=40 |pages=73–140 |doi=10.2307/2843145 |jstor=2843145 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pauly |first=Antonio |date=1928 |title=Ensayo de etnografía americana: viajes y exploraciones |url=https://scholar.googleusercontent.com/scholar.bib?q=info:9C8Le6CAD4MJ:scholar.google.com/&output=citation&scisdr=ClFwSG4NEKCZ3srkzXA:AFWwaeYAAAAAZmHi1XAa-vGiXpqkbSIAQZItpeI&scisig=AFWwaeYAAAAAZmHi1Z5iktlbscHc1vXXRVvH5aQ&scisf=4&ct=citation&cd=-1&hl=es |journal=(No Title)}}</ref>

== Morphology ==
As far as nominal morphology is concerned, non-human nouns seem to carry the suffix {{lang|caz|-ni}}, which probably indicates the non-possessed form of the noun. For example, the nouns {{lang|caz|ni-chi}} 'smoke', {{lang|caz|ni-chuku}} 'fire', and {{lang|caz|ni-platsu}} 'flower'. Some adjectives also carry the prefix {{lang|caz|-ni}}, e.g. {{lang|caz|ni'-tatila}} 'canine', {{lang|caz|nĩ'-bla'su}} 'boy, small'. Nouns not bearing this prefix are those referring to kinship terms and body parts, which are always inalienable nouns bearing a personal prefix; for example: the nouns {{lang|caz|eu-tana}} 'my mother' and {{lang|caz|eu-nimara}} 'my heart'. As far as number is concerned, the plural is expressed by the suffix {{lang|caz|-na}}, e.g. {{lang|caz|santo-na}} 'saints'.

As for verbal morphology, it can only be noted that the main arguments S and A of the first and second person are obligatorily marked in the verb. The personal prefixes S/A seem to be derived from the free personal pronouns and can also appear in nouns as possessive markers, as observed in (1).
{{Interlinear|Eu-tarpa eu-ja-tissi Dios|1SG-love 1SG-HON-father God|I love God (lit. I love my father God)
| number = (1)
| lang1 = caz
}}
As for the negation, it seems that this is not marked in the predicate but is only expressed through the negative particle ''nihuas'', which is placed before the predicate, as observed in (2):<ref name=":0" />

{{Interlinear|Nihuas e-massota en-copphurúnue|NEG 1SG-understand 2SG-language|I don't understand your language
| number = (2)
| lang1 = caz
}}

== Syntax ==
As in neighboring languages, it seems that the only obligatory element in the Canichana clause is the predicate, which generally precedes the subject and complements, as seen in (3):

{{Interlinear|E-massota en-copphurúnue|1SG-understand 2SG-language|I understand your language
| number = (3)
| lang1 = caz
}}

Interrogative pronouns always appear in the initial position of the phrase, as seen in (4):

{{Interlinear|Lava an-ja-chi?|where 2SG-go-*|Where are you going?
| number = (4)
| lang1 = caz
}}

In the noun phrase, the adjectives follow the core noun, as seen in (5):<ref name=":0" />

{{Interlinear|nérahua mátihi|banana ripe|ripe banana
| number = (5)
| lang1 = caz
}}

==Language contact==
Jolkesky (2016) notes that there are lexical similarities with the [[Mochica language]] due to contact.<ref name="Jolkesky-2016">{{cite thesis|last=Jolkesky |first=Marcelo Pinho de Valhery |date=2016 |url=http://www.etnolinguistica.org/tese:jolkesky-2016-arqueoecolinguistica |title=Estudo arqueo-ecolinguístico das terras tropicais sul-americanas |type=Ph.D. dissertation |location=Brasília |publisher=University of Brasília |edition=2}}</ref>
